text:
on worry, and the general laws and operations of the mind, Schopenhauer is as precise as anyone I've come across

here he lays out why the mind can never seem to be fully free from care

when one worry lifts: "...another immediately takes its place. The whole material of this already existed previously, yet it could not enter consciousness as care, because the consciousness had no capacity left for it."

It had remained merely as a dark and unobserved misty form on the extreme horizon of consciousness.

But now, as there is room, this ready material at once comes forward and occupies the throne of the reigning care of the day.

If so far as its matter is concerned it is very much lighter than the material of the care that has vanished, it knows how to blow itself out, so that it apparently equals it in size, and thus, as the chief care of the day, completely fills the throne."

--

if I had to try and sum that up -- when you have big worries, the small worries disappear. there's no room for them, no capacity.

when your big worries are solved, your small worries magically reappear - they were the "unobserved misty form on the extreme horizon of consciousness."

and in that final paragraph he addresses how they "blow themselves out to completely fill the throne."

I'm not that bright but when I first read this, years back, it knocked a lot of things into place. The rich have never been happier than the poor, because the mind never settles... it just creates new worries that "fill the throne." 

A bunch of stuff in this article rearranges your mental walk-in closet like that -- it can be thick but is worth the time.
